# Puntland formation — source clarification for later authoring

Puntland’s formation should be dated to **August 1998**, as an autonomous administration within Somalia. The 2001 UNDP report dates formation to that month and describes the provisional charter’s commitment to Somali unity. Walter Kälin’s 2010 UN mission report likewise places the declaration of an autonomous region within Somalia in 1998.¹ ²

This resolves the bounded source question raised by the World Bank report’s 1993 date and its 1998 “independence” wording. Use the UN reports for the formation statement and keep the World Bank wording as source provenance. This correction does not determine current political status, territorial boundaries or any particular displacement event. The original 1998 charter and an exact formation day were not inspected or accepted here.

The UNDP report names Mark Bradbury, Ken Menkhaus and Roland Marchal as authors, with Bradbury also coordinating editor. Its methodology combines existing studies and interviews. Its acknowledgements credit financial support from Denmark through DANIDA; production, design, editing and Somali-overview translation are separate credits. This is an institutional synthesis with disclosed support, not an inspection of the original constitutional instrument.¹

Kälin’s report records a 14–21 October 2009 mission and carries a 21 January 2010 document date. The downloaded edition has Arabic front matter and an English annex. The mission visited northern settlements and interviewed arrivals from the south, but security prevented travel to south-central Somalia and limited government consultations. Its retrospective 1998 statement is not a claim that the mission observed Puntland’s founding.²

**Grounding and limits:** nine UNDP and four HRC original page images were read, including source identity, relevant credits/methods and the cited passages. Neither entire report was read. No full charter, current constitution, independent field data or new population count was verified. The main-agent review supports this source note; independent case and statistical acceptance remain separate. No event, score, geometry, incoming-flight note, global bibliography ID or publication was changed.

Author/method and acknowledgement pages: PDF 6 and 15–17. [Official UN copy](https://somalia.un.org/en/download/7250/34529). Accessed 11 September 2026.
2. Walter Kälin, *Report…on his mission to Somalia (14–21 October 2009)*, A/HRC/13/21/Add.2, 21 January 2010, English annex paragraph 4, printed/PDF 4; mission scope paragraphs 1–3. [Official UN copy, Arabic front matter with English annex](https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/g10/103/94/pdf/g1010394.pdf). Accessed 11 September 2026.

# Three Gorges — later evidence for authoring

The inspected sources support compulsory relocation and uneven livelihood outcomes. **The event’s saved 1994–2012 endpoints and a fully reconciled final displacement total remain unresolved.** This note supplements the corrected Cernea citation; it does not change the frozen event.

The State Council’s 2001 regulation required people and organizations designated for relocation to move; Article 31 prohibited refusal or delay, with sanctions addressed in Article 58. Articles 3, 5 and 7 set out livelihood-restoration goals, compensation and subsequent support. These provisions establish the policy framework, not whether each household received adequate compensation. The consent clauses in Articles 12 and 18 concern household-registration conversion and joint house construction, respectively; they do not make the overall relocation voluntary. The regulation was promulgated on 15 February 2001 and took effect on 1 March, replacing the 1993 regulation. The National Energy Administration’s 19 August 2011 page date is a later hosting date.¹

The National Audit Office reported **1,296,400 people** in its relocation-and-housing category by the end of 2011, against a plan of **1,245,500**. This is a government-reported administrative total with a stated cutoff, not an independently reconstructed census. The audit covered draft financial accounts and distinguished construction, resettlement-fund and reporting dates. Its regional income indicators cannot establish every resettled household’s outcome. Its indexed later sections also record compensation-related petitions, funding irregularities and continuing support needs; its opening statement about rectification should not become a claim that every household’s grievance was resolved. The provincial republication available through the web reader ends before those later sections; the central-government indexed extracts preserve them. A complete original audit body was not captured.²

Brooke Wilmsen reports improved livelihoods alongside persistent disadvantages for rural-to-urban households in Badong and Zigui. **351 of 521 households** responded in 2012/13 about 2011 conditions; the 2003/04 questionnaire also sought retrospective accounts around 1998. Keep this sample, nonresponse and the distinction between correlation and causation explicit.³

The April 2017 compendium contains presentation summaries and acknowledges ADB, World Bank and Philippine Learning Center support. These event credits establish neither study funding nor independence. Wilmsen’s summary has no study-specific disclosure and cites a differently titled 2016 article whose full text remains uninspected.³

The earlier Cernea tables contain different forecasts. Their difference remains unexplained; neither should be silently replaced by the later administrative count. The inspected sources do not settle the first and last displacement dates for the saved event. Dates of regulations, surveys, construction or account closure are not substitutes. The next historical review must specify which relocation cohort and date convention it is assessing.
